channel.description: Recent content in masks on darktable user manual

item.title: overview
item.description:
Masks allow you to limit the effect of a module so that it only applies to certain parts of the image.

A mask can be regarded as a grayscale image where each pixel has a value between 0 and 1.0 (or between 0% and 100%). This value is the opacity and is used to determine how much a module affects each pixel. Where the mask is 0 the module has no effect; where it is 1.0 the module has its full effect.

item.title: the mask panel
item.description:
The mask panel is where a module’s blending and masking are controlled. It holds everything needed to build a mask: creating shapes and parametric elements, importing masks from other modules, arranging elements into groups, choosing operators, and refining the result.

From top to bottom, the panel is made of:

  1. the panel header, with the mask on/off toggle and the display and editing buttons;
  2. the blending controls (blend mode, opacity);
  3. the mask layout: the tree of groups and elements that make up the mask;
  4. the selection caption, naming the selected member;
  5. the toolbar, to add groups, shapes and parametric elements and to import from other modules;
  6. the controls of the selected member;
  7. the help, refinements and mask consumers sections.

#panel position

When moved from its default position under the module (see the panel position options), the mask panel displays the mask of the focused module.

item.title: groups & operators
item.description:
A mask is a tree of groups. Each group combines its members – elements and other groups – with a single operator. This page explains the operators, and how to arrange groups to get the mask you want.

#the one rule

A group is a stack of members whose interaction is governed by the group’s operator. A group starts from its bottom member and applies its operator to each member above it in turn, in the same way as modules are applied in the pixelpipe. A member can be an element or another group: once a group has been computed, its result is used by the group above as if it were a single element, in the same way as brackets work in arithmetic.

item.title: drawn shapes
item.description: Drawn shapes are mask elements that you draw directly on the image: brush strokes, circles, ellipses, paths and gradients. Like any element, a shape can be combined with other elements in groups, and it can be reused in other modules. AI objects are created in the same way, but differ from other shapes in that, by default, they are stored as pixels (a raster) and not as editable outlines – see how AI objects are stored.

item.title: parametric elements
item.description:
Parametric elements offer fine-grained selective control over how individual pixels are masked, based on their values rather than on their location. Each parametric element selects a range of values of one data channel (e.g. lightness, hue or the red channel) and assigns each pixel an opacity between 0 and 1 (100%) depending on its value in that channel.

A single element works on a single channel. To select pixels by several criteria, add several elements and combine them in a group: with an intersection operator (minimum or product), only pixels that match all elements are selected; with a union operator (maximum or screen), pixels that match any element are selected. The same channel can be used by several elements, for example to select two separate ranges of hue.

item.title: raster masks
item.description:
The final output of a module’s mask (the combined effect of all of its elements, refinements and opacity) is a grayscale raster image representing the extent to which the module’s effect is applied to each pixel. This raster image is stored internally for active modules, and can be reused by other modules later in the pixelpipe as a raster mask element.

As with any element, if the opacity value for a pixel in a raster mask is zero, it does not select that pixel; if the opacity is 1.0 it fully selects it. A raster mask can be combined with other elements – including other raster masks – using groups & operators, and it can be inverted, refined and given its own opacity, like any other element. For example, you can intersect the mask of an earlier module with a luminance range, or subtract a drawn shape from it.

item.title: AI masking
item.description:
AI masking requires AI features to be enabled in AI preferences, with a model active for the mask task. See the AI features overview for what runs where.

#AI object

The AI object tool selects an object for you: instead of drawing its outline by hand, click on the subject and a segmentation model produces the mask. An AI object is an element like any other: it can be combined with other elements in groups, inverted, refined, and given its own opacity.

item.title: refinements
item.description:
The refinements section of the mask panel contains sliders that further refine a mask: they select by the amount of detail, align the mask’s edges with the image, blur it, or change its tonal response.

Refinements are not limited to the final mask. They act on whatever is selected in the mask layout:

  • with an element selected, they refine that element alone, before it is combined with the other members of its group;
  • with a group selected, they refine the group’s result, after its operator has combined its members;
  • with the whole mask selected (nothing else selected), they refine the final mask of the module.

This allows, for example, feathering only the drawn part of a mask while leaving its parametric part untouched, or applying the details threshold to a single branch of the mask.

item.title: group layout presets
item.description:
A group layout preset is a ready-made arrangement of groups and operators, without any elements in it. Presets set up common masks in one click, and the built-in ones come with notes explaining how to use them. You can also save the layout of any group as a preset of your own, and use it in any module.

#applying a preset

Select a group (or the whole mask) and click the presets button in the selection caption of the mask panel. The popover lists the built-in presets followed by your user defined presets. Hover over a preset’s name to see an outline of its groups, operators and opacities.

item.title: migrating from classic masks
item.description:
The masking system of darktable was redesigned after version 5.6. This section is for users who know the previous (“classic”) system. It explains what happens to existing edits and how familiar workflows translate to the mask panel.

Important: The conversion is one way. Once an edit has been saved by the new version of darktable, older versions cannot read its masks: darktable 5.6 and earlier report a mask version mismatch and drop every mask of that image. If you may still want to open your edits with an older version, back up your library database and XMP sidecar files first.
